canonical_topic: Base load power and the three-tier capacity structure
definition: Base load power is the minimum level of demand a grid must supply at essentially all times; it anchors how much always-on generation capacity a region needs, with additional tiers of capacity layered on top for variable and peak demand.
core_idea: Using historical hourly load data (the PJM-West example, Jan 2004-Aug 2006), the author shows demand never fell below roughly 20,000 MWh, was above 30,000 MWh about half the time, and peaked near 60,000 MWh, illustrating how a cumulative load distribution is used to size three tiers of generation capacity.
key_points: Base load power = the minimum amount of power that must be supplied to the grid at any given time; base load power plants are the units sized to run full-time to meet it.
A cumulative load distribution (percentage of time load exceeds a given level) is a practical tool for estimating capacity needs from historical hourly demand.
PJM-West example: load never below ~20,000 MWh, above 30,000 MWh about half the time, above 40,000 MWh only about 10% of the time, peaks near 60,000 MWh.
Roughly 20,000 MWh of capacity should be base load: highly efficient, low-cost units that benefit from running around the clock.
Roughly another 20,000 MWh should be intermediate/variable capacity: units cycled on and off regularly but used fairly often.
Roughly another 20,000 MWh should be peaking capacity: units that run less than 10% of the year, so the priority for them is being cheap to build, store, and start rather than efficient to run.
relationships: Derived from the region's cumulative load distribution
Complements customer-class segmentation and temperature-driven demand analysis
trading_implications: The proportion of time a region spends at different load levels indicates how much cheap base load vs. flexible/peaking capacity a market needs, which shapes the economics and dispatch order of different plant types.
caveats: The specific 20,000/20,000/20,000 MWh split is illustrative for the PJM-West example given, not a universal rule for all grids.
